section_summary: This section traces disputes over the destruction, temporary use, and four-power division of Japanese naval vessels after the war. Soviet representatives sought ships for Soviet-controlled areas, joint inventories, and an end to the use of allocable ships for repatriation; U.S. officials insisted on specific shipping needs and SCAP control. British discussions raised possible shares for France and the Netherlands. The section ends with vessel inventories and a January 1947 policy report setting out a U.S.-managed division procedure.

subfiles.title: Agreement on disposition of Japanese naval vessels
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department gives the dates and status of four-power consultations on destroying or dividing Japanese warships.
subfiles.summary: The USSR endorsed the general principles in October 1945, while Britain had not formally replied. The Department describes subsequent notes to the Soviet Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Request for dates of Allied agreement
subfiles.to: War Department and Secretary of State
subfiles.about: SCAP requests information after the Soviet Allied Council member questions warship disposition.
subfiles.summary: Requests dates of four-power agreement and updates on Soviet negotiations.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Soviet communication delivered
subfiles.about: The embassy reports delivery of a supplementary communication on the Japanese fleet.
subfiles.summary: A supplementary letter on fleet disposition was given to Lozovski on May 8.

subfiles.title: Soviet Protest in Connection with SCAP Directive on Destruction of Japanese Naval Vessels
subfiles.about: Atcheson forwards five documents and explains the Soviet objections to SCAP’s destruction directive.
subfiles.summary: He outlines Derevyanko’s demands concerning consultation, observers, target ships, inventories, auxiliaries, repatriation, and ammunition. Atcheson argues that the protest seeks to expand the Allied Council’s authority and protect ships sought by the USSR.

subfiles.title: Destruction of Former Japanese Naval Vessels
subfiles.about: SCAP orders the scrapping or other approved destruction of specified large surface combatants.
subfiles.summary: Orders eligible vessels destroyed within one year and requires plans and progress reports.

subfiles.title: Information Pertaining to SCAPIN 910
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains the authority and administrative roles behind the ship-destruction directive.
subfiles.summary: Explains JCS authority, SCAP oversight, and naval and army responsibilities.

subfiles.title: Soviet objections to the naval-vessel directive
subfiles.about: Derevyanko sets out Soviet objections and proposals concerning the destruction and allocation of Japanese naval vessels.
subfiles.summary: He challenges the short consultation period and requests observers, destruction records, target ships, a four-power inventory committee, preservation of allocable ships, and destruction of naval facilities and ammunition.

subfiles.title: Reply to Derevyanko on destruction of naval vessels
subfiles.about: Mueller explains SCAP’s authority and answers the proposed four-power executive committee.
subfiles.summary: Says policy questions exceed SCAP’s authority and current repatriation and submarine destruction follow instructions.

subfiles.title: Protest over Allied Council consultation
subfiles.about: Derevyanko protests issuance of Directive 910 before his recommendations were considered.
subfiles.summary: He asks that proposed directives on essential matters be discussed by the Allied Council as a body and that recommendations be presented in its name.

subfiles.title: Atcheson’s reply on Allied Council procedure
subfiles.about: Atcheson defends SCAP’s handling of the directive and individual consultation with council members.
subfiles.summary: He says the four governments agreed on basic principles, MacArthur considered the Soviet views, and meetings for every directive would be impracticable. Individual consultation permits both separate and joint views.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Despatch No. 419 to War Department
subfiles.about: Lyon transmits Atcheson’s despatch on the Soviet protest.
subfiles.summary: Forwards a copy of Despatch No. 419.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Despatch No. 419 to Navy Department
subfiles.about: Lyon transmits the Soviet-protest despatch and enclosures to the Navy Department.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Despatch No. 419 and its enclosures.

subfiles.title: Disposition of Japanese Merchant Fleet
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews U.S. statements and Soviet proposals concerning Japanese merchant and naval shipping.
subfiles.summary: It says no agreement to divide the merchant fleet exists and its final disposition awaits Far Eastern Commission policy. It proposes referring the Soviet note to SWNCC and seeking clarification about ships already in Soviet hands.

subfiles.title: Referral of Soviet ship-allocation reply to SWNCC
subfiles.about: Hilldring requests study of the Soviet reply on Japanese naval and merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: Refers the enclosed Moscow telegram to the Far East subcommittee.

subfiles.title: Lozovski’s reply on Japanese naval and merchant fleets
subfiles.about: The embassy transmits Lozovski’s June 1 letter proposing commissions and changes to repatriation shipping.
subfiles.summary: The Soviet government says Derevyanko supplied ship data to SCAP. It proposes four-power commissions to inventory naval and merchant vessels and asks that allocable warships be released from repatriation duties.

subfiles.title: Atcheson’s appeal for Soviet repatriation cooperation
subfiles.about: Atcheson reports a letter urging Soviet authorities to deliver detained Japanese to repatriation ports.
subfiles.summary: The letter argues that faster repatriation would free Japanese ships for final disposition. It contrasts progress from other Allied-controlled areas with the absence of repatriation from Soviet-controlled areas and seeks a Soviet response by the next Allied Council meeting.

subfiles.title: Soviet Request for Allocation of Japanese Navy and Merchant Vessels
subfiles.about: Atcheson forwards a Soviet ship request and his reply requiring specific purposes and SCAP control.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the June 3 request and June 14 reply; no Soviet answer had arrived.

subfiles.title: Request for ships for Soviet-command tasks
subfiles.about: Derevyanko requests specified categories and numbers of Japanese naval and merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: Lists requested vessels and seeks their transfer before final Allied distribution.

subfiles.title: Reply to Soviet request for Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: Atcheson asks for specific tasks before SCAP considers assigning ships to Soviet-command areas.
subfiles.summary: Says ships remain needed for repatriation and any assignment would remain under SCAP control.

subfiles.title: Soviet Embassy note on allocation of Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: The Soviet Embassy objects to Atcheson’s reply and requests U.S. instructions for allocating ships to Soviet-command tasks.
subfiles.summary: The Russian original is followed by an English translation. The note recalls the April U.S. proposal, characterizes Atcheson’s demand for specific purposes as a negative answer, and urges instructions to MacArthur.

subfiles.title: Analysis of the Soviet Embassy’s ship-allocation note
subfiles.about: Emmerson explains why SCAP requires fuller Soviet shipping data and proposes a reply.
subfiles.summary: He contrasts the Soviet July note with the May U.S. clarification, arguing that Soviet ship requests state only vague purposes and incomplete holdings. His proposed reply asks for enough information to make an equitable assignment.

subfiles.title: British notes of conversation on dividing Japanese warships
subfiles.about: Britain accepts equal four-power division but asks about shares for France and the Netherlands.
subfiles.summary: Britain proposes sharing its quarter with Commonwealth partners and asks whether the United States will allocate ships to France and the Netherlands.

subfiles.title: Proposed procedure for disposal of Japanese destroyers
subfiles.about: The note proposes delaying division until SCAP releases ships from occupation tasks.
subfiles.summary: Seeks British agreement to four-power division after repatriation and minesweeping needs end.

subfiles.title: Rough estimate of allocable Japanese ships
subfiles.about: The estimate counts Japanese ships potentially within the destroyer-and-smaller allocation category.
subfiles.summary: Lists ship types and rough quantities as of January 1946.

subfiles.title: British Representations Regarding Division of Japanese Combatant Vessels
subfiles.about: Emmerson reviews possible U.S. allocations to France and the Netherlands and drafts a response to Britain.
subfiles.summary: He notes a prior U.S. agreement in principle to transfer part of its share to France. No Dutch request was known, but he suggests the United States could consider a Dutch allocation.

subfiles.title: Conversation on British representations regarding Japanese combatants
subfiles.about: Vincent answers Graves on delivery plans and possible French and Dutch shares.
subfiles.summary: Records SCAP’s readiness to release a first lot and the U.S. position on France and the Netherlands.

subfiles.title: British request for source of Dutch ministerial statement
subfiles.about: Britain asks for a reference to the Dutch statement declining Japanese naval vessels.
subfiles.summary: Requests the source of the Netherlands navy minister’s reported statement.

subfiles.title: Reply on Dutch ministerial statement
subfiles.about: The Department identifies the date and substance of the Dutch navy minister’s statement.
subfiles.summary: Reports that J. N. de Booy said on January 18 that integrating Japanese ships was impracticable.

subfiles.title: SWNCC transmittal on disposition of Japanese combatant vessels
subfiles.about: SWNCC forwards its approved policy report and vessel lists for diplomatic and SCAP action.
subfiles.summary: Requests notes to Britain, China, and the USSR and forwards vessel lists.

subfiles.title: Enclosure A: operable ex-Japanese Navy ships
subfiles.about: The inventory lists destroyer-size-and-smaller vessels operable or repairable within sixty days.
subfiles.summary: Lists destroyers, escorts, patrol craft, minelayers, minesweepers, transports, rescue boats, and auxiliaries. Service codes indicate SCAP shipping or minesweeping use.

subfiles.title: Enclosure B: available ships divided into four lots
subfiles.about: The list arranges currently available Japanese destroyers and escorts into four equal lots.
subfiles.summary: Sets out four lots of sixteen ships each.

subfiles.title: Enclosure C: wrecked or long-repair ex-Japanese Navy ships
subfiles.about: The inventory locates smaller Japanese combatant vessels that are wrecked, sunk, or need more than sixty days of repair.
subfiles.summary: Lists destroyers, escorts, patrol craft, subchasers, minelayers, minesweepers, transports, and rescue boats by location or as unlocated.

subfiles.title: File note for SWNCC letter
subfiles.about: The note identifies the SWNCC letter on Japanese combatant-vessel disposition.
subfiles.summary: Identifies the January 10 SWNCC letter filed here.

subfiles.title: SWNCC 186/23: Disposition of Combatant Vessels of the Japanese Navy
subfiles.from: State-War-Navy Coordinating Subcommittee for the Far East
subfiles.about: The report sets a U.S. position on Soviet proposals and a procedure for dividing allocable Japanese combatants.
subfiles.summary: The report rejects Soviet proposals for four-power inventory commissions and for removing allocable ships from repatriation and other occupation duties. It recommends that the United States determine available ships, form four equal lots, and arrange delivery outside Japan as SCAP releases vessels. Its appendices summarize prior agreements, SCAP authority, ship categories, merchant-fleet policy, Soviet requests, and repatriation developments. Pages 136–137, 139–140, 141–142, 143–144, and 146–147 contain overlapping or duplicate text in this copy; the discussion continues beyond page 147.
